questions.q: Modern forensic DNA profiling relies heavily on the analysis of STRs. What does the acronym STR stand for?
options: Standard Truncated Regions
Short Tandem Repeats
Specific Targeted Replicas
Synthesized Template Receptors
questions.explain: STR stands for Short Tandem Repeats, which are repeating sequences of 3 to 7 base pairs in the non-coding regions of DNA. Source: Analysis - STRs (Short Tandem Repeats).

questions.q: Why have Short Tandem Repeats (STRs) largely replaced Restriction Fragment Length Polymorphisms (RFLPs) in forensic DNA analysis?
options: STRs contain the entire coding sequence for structural genes, whereas RFLPs only contain 'junk' DNA.
STRs are much shorter lengths of DNA, making them far less susceptible to degradation and ideal for amplification via PCR.
STR loci are found in mitochondrial DNA, while RFLPs are restricted strictly to nuclear DNA.
STR analysis requires large, intact biological samples, which guarantees a pristine DNA profile.
questions.explain: Because STRs are short (usually under 450 base pairs long), they are less likely to break down in degraded samples compared to the long fragments required for RFLP, and they are easily amplified using PCR.

questions.q: In an STR region of DNA, individual variations arise primarily due to differences in the:
options: Number of times a short DNA sequence repeats itself.
Chemical composition of the sugar-phosphate backbone.
Substitution of Uracil in place of Thymine.
Location of the sequence on mitochondrial instead of nuclear chromosomes.
questions.explain: STR polymorphism is based on length; individuals differ in how many times the short sequence pattern repeats. For example, one person may have 8 repeats, while another has 12.

questions.q: Gel electrophoresis is a critical technique used to separate and analyze DNA fragments post-PCR. What physical property does the gel matrix utilize to separate the fragments?
options: Base pair chemistry (A-T vs C-G ratio)
Magnetic resonance
Size (length) of the DNA fragments
Thermal conductivity of the nucleotides
questions.explain: Gel electrophoresis separates DNA fragments by size. The porous gel acts as a sieve, allowing fragments to move based on their length. Source: Gel Electrophoresis (smaller fragments move faster).

questions.subject: Forensic Science

questions.q: During gel electrophoresis, DNA molecules are pushed through the gel by an electrical current. In which direction do the DNA fragments migrate, and why?
options: Toward the positive pole (anode) because DNA possesses a net negative charge.
Toward the negative pole (cathode) because DNA possesses a net positive charge.
Toward the positive pole (anode) because DNA relies on positive hydrogen bonds.
They move in both directions randomly until the electrical current separates them.
questions.explain: The phosphate groups in the DNA backbone give the molecule a net negative electrical charge. Consequently, when placed in an electric field, DNA migrates toward the positively charged electrode (anode). Source: Gel Electrophoresis (DNA moves toward the positive pole).

questions.q: In a completed gel electrophoresis run, analyzing the migration distances reveals the sizes of different fragments. Which statement accurately describes this migration?
options: Larger DNA fragments migrate faster and travel further through the gel than smaller ones.
Smaller DNA fragments experience less resistance and migrate faster, traveling further through the gel.
All DNA fragments migrate at the exact same speed; their final position depends on original volume.
DNA fragments do not migrate unless treated with specialized radioactive isotopes.
questions.explain: The gel matrix acts as a molecular sieve. Smaller DNA fragments thread through the pores easier and migrate faster/further than larger, bulkier fragments. Source: Gel Electrophoresis (smaller fragments move faster).

questions.q: What is the purpose of running a 'DNA ladder' or 'allelic ladder' alongside crime scene samples during electrophoresis?
options: To provide DNA fragments of known lengths used as standard references to determine the sizes of the unknown fragments.
To ensure the electrical current remains positive throughout the entire run.
To actively stain the DNA so it glows under ultraviolet light.
To extract any remaining nucleases that could degrade the sample.
questions.explain: A DNA ladder is a mixture of standard DNA fragments with known base-pair sizes. By comparing unknown sample bands to the ladder, the scientist can calculate the size of the STR alleles.

questions.q: When viewing an STR DNA profile, a locus shows two distinct peaks (bands) at the D3S1358 marker. What does this indicate about the individual's genotype for that specific STR?
options: The individual is homozygous at that locus, having inherited identical alleles from both parents.
The individual is heterozygous at that locus, having inherited a different number of repeats from each parent.
The DNA sample is highly degraded and missing data.
The DNA represents mitochondrial contamination.
questions.explain: If a locus displays two different peaks or bands, the individual is heterozygous, meaning they inherited a different allele (e.g., 14 repeats and 16 repeats) from each parent for that specific genetic marker.

questions.q: If a person is homozygous at a specific STR locus, what pattern will appear on their electropherogram or gel for that locus?
options: A single, taller peak or single thick band.
Two peaks of completely unequal heights.
A complete absence of any peaks or bands.
A minimum of four distinct peaks representing the maternal and paternal lines.
questions.explain: Homozygous means inheriting identical alleles from both parents. During analysis, they migrate to the same spot, resulting in one single prominent band on a gel or one large peak on an electropherogram.

questions.q: While analyzing a 20-locus STR profile for CODIS entry, one particular locus called 'Amelogenin' is always included. What does the Amelogenin gene specifically determine in a forensic context?
options: The race or ethnic background of the donor.
The approximate age of the biological donor.
The biological sex of the individual.
The exact maternal lineage.
questions.explain: The Amelogenin locus is the standard sex-determining marker used in multiplex STR kits. A female profile will display XX, whereas a male profile displays XY.

questions.q: Modern forensic laboratories extract, amplify, and visualize multiple STR loci simultaneously in a single reaction tube. What is the correct scientific term for this process?
options: Capillary sequencing
Southern Blotting
Multiplexing
Heteroplasmy
questions.explain: Multiplexing is the process where PCR kits are designed to amplify 20+ STR loci simultaneously using different fluorescent dye labels, allowing massive amounts of data to be gleaned from one trace sample.

questions.q: In a modern DNA laboratory, traditional gel slabs are frequently replaced by a method utilizing thin glass tubes and lasers to read fluorescently tagged DNA fragments in real-time. This technique is called:
options: Gas Chromatography-Mass Spectrometry (GC-MS)
Capillary Electrophoresis (CE)
Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM)
Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy (FTIR)
questions.explain: Capillary Electrophoresis uses narrow tubes and automated laser detection to resolve the sizes of STRs much faster and more accurately than traditional slab gels.

questions.q: When generating a DNA profile, how do forensic scientists mathematically determine the random match probability—the chance that an unrelated person shares the same 20-locus profile?
options: By adding the frequencies of all the alleles present at the 20 loci.
By dividing the total population by the number of alleles found.
By using the product rule to multiply the frequencies of independently occurring alleles across all tested loci.
By running the sample through CODIS and counting the number of false hits.
questions.explain: The product rule asserts that one can calculate the overall probability of a combined genetic profile by multiplying together the individual population frequencies of each allele present at independent loci.

questions.q: If a gel electrophoresis run is left running for far too long, what adverse consequence will most likely occur?
options: The gel will permanently mutate the DNA sequence into a new locus.
The smaller DNA fragments will migrate completely off the end of the gel and be lost into the buffer solution.
The DNA fragments will reverse their charge and migrate backward toward the negative pole.
The DNA fragments will fuse back together forming one massive chromosome.
questions.explain: Because smaller fragments migrate the fastest toward the anode, excessive running time will push them entirely off the far edge of the gel matrix into the liquid buffer, losing the data.
